entries.question: How does artificial light cancel or dominate the light coming from stars?
entries.heat: stackexchange/physics snapshot 2026-10-08: 10 votes, 6 comments (live check unavailable 2026-10-09, sources unreachable)
entries.answer_md: Artificial light does not cancel starlight; it raises the sky background against which stars have to be seen. Scattering in the atmosphere spreads lamplight into a broad skyglow, so the contrast between a star and its surroundings falls, and faint stars disappear first because stars are near point sources while skyglow fills the whole field of view. A camera can partly recover the signal by narrowing its field of view and integrating longer, which is why observatories are sited far from cities. In our fiction, the Type-II superlattice perception matrix treats that same contrast problem as solved by an artificial InAs/GaSb crystal with an engineered band structure; that architecture is a **setting**, not a demonstrated device.

entries.question: How can a person show/present a nonlinear time
entries.heat: stackexchange/worldbuilding snapshot 2026-10-08: -2 votes, 1 comment (low-vote long tail; live check unavailable 2026-10-09)
entries.answer_md: Nonlinear time is not an established physical entity: in physics time is normally a coordinate or a parameter, and rewriting it is a change of description rather than a new substance. Relativity does make elapsed time observer-dependent, since proper time follows a worldline, but that is curvature and motion rather than a narrative loop. What is firmly real is that time can be used as a control knob: periodically driving a system is standard **Floquet engineering**, and the driven system acquires quasi-energy structure that static matter does not have. In our fiction, temporally programmed matter is written as a phase a machine can set; that programmability is a **setting**, not an engineering capability.
